chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to me who said: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi narrated to me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, on the authority of Muawiyah ibn Wahb, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) that he said:

O Muawiyah! Whoever is granted three things is not deprived of three things: Whoever is granted the ability to supplicate is granted the response; whoever is granted gratitude is granted increase; and whoever is granted reliance is granted sufficiency.

For indeed Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, says in His Book: 'And whoever puts his trust in Allah, then He is sufficient for him'; and He says: 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]'; and He says: 'Call upon Me; I will respond to you.'

key_terms.الْإِجَابَةُ: The response or acceptance of the supplication
key_terms.الْكَفَالَةُ: Sufficiency or being enough for one's needs

ai.seo_question: What are the three things that, if granted, ensure one is not deprived of their corresponding rewards?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal-Khisal*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) outlines a spiritual reciprocity where supplication, gratitude, and reliance on God yield answered prayers, increased blessings, and divine sufficiency respectively. This teaching is deeply rooted in Shia theological emphasis on the interplay between human agency and divine grace, highlighting that these virtues are not merely acts of worship but mechanisms for sustaining spiritual and material prosperity. The narration underscores the practical application of tawakkul as an active trust rather than passive resignation, a key concept in Shia ethical thought.
